strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: inadequate exploration in classifier-based Bayesian optimization. Combining BORE-style acquisition with label propagation or label spreading is a simple, potentially useful contribution, despite relying on established components.

The evaluation covers both sampled unlabeled points and fixed candidate pools, including synthetic functions, tabular hyperparameter optimization, NATS-Bench, and image embeddings. Twenty repeated runs with standard-error bands provide meaningful empirical evidence, with substantial improvements on synthetic benchmarks and faster progress on NATS-Bench against the tested baselines.

The connection to BORE and LFBO is explained, and the appendices investigate bandwidth, sampling distributions, unlabeled sample counts, pool subsampling, and threshold ratios. Appendix D appropriately acknowledges that existing semi-supervised learning guarantees do not directly apply to this sequential setting.
weaknesses: The central contribution is not adequately isolated. The comparison without unlabeled data in Figure 12 fixes β = 0.5, whereas the headline experiments learn β at every iteration. Moreover, the labeled-only kernel estimator performs competitively or better in several ablation panels, including Bukin6 and Branin with label spreading. A labeled-only kernel baseline with matched or comparably tuned bandwidths, together with an ablation of random tie-breaking, is needed to establish how much improvement actually comes from label propagation.

The proposed explanation for improved exploration remains speculative. Sampling truncated Gaussians around observed points does not ensure Assumption 4.1: objective-threshold labels can change within high-density regions. Likewise, expanding the favorable decision region does not establish that maximizing class probability explores effectively. Appendix D neither establishes the asserted margin reduction nor connects it to optimization performance. Direct measurements of exploration or escape from local optima would strengthen this central claim.

The acquisition-search protocol is insufficiently specified to assess the comparisons confidently. Section 5 describes L-BFGS-B with 1,000 starts, but does not clearly explain maximization over finite pools or optimization of the piecewise-constant tree-based classifiers. Candidate eligibility, exclusion of previously evaluated points, and application of the tie-breaking heuristic across methods also need clarification. These choices can materially affect apparent stagnation. A random-search baseline would provide an additional useful reference.

The evidence for broader applicability is limited. Continuous optimization is tested only on four two-dimensional functions. The 64-dimensional MNIST experiment uses representations trained on 440,000 labeled examples of the same digit-recognition task that defines the objective. Although the representation is shared across methods and the data splits are separate, this supplies substantial task-specific supervision. A baseline that ranks candidates using the already-trained classifier would help establish what additional optimization contributes.

Reproduction requires several correctable details: input scaling, the label-spreading clamping factor, propagation stopping settings, and initialization and bounds for bandwidth optimization are not clearly reported. There is also an algebraic inconsistency in Section 4.1: the stated column-normalized definition of p_ij implies P = WD⁻¹, whereas the text gives P = D⁻¹W and subsequently propagates with Pᵀ. The intended convention and implemented update should be reconciled.
